Shake
shāk
v.t. & v.i. (to agitate, to cause to tremble; rendering Hebrew ra'ash, Greek seiō, saleuō)
Saxon sceacan, to move violently to and fro. Scripture's shakings are deliberate divine acts that test what is founded and remove what is not.

Biblical Definition

God shakes on purpose, and Hebrews explains the purpose. Quoting Haggai — “Yet once, it is a little while, and I will shake the heavens, and the earth, and the sea, and the dry land” (Hag 2:6) — the writer says, “Whose voice then shook the earth: but now he hath promised, saying, Yet once more I shake not the earth only, but also heaven” (Heb 12:26), and draws the conclusion that the shaking removes what can be shaken so that what cannot be shaken may remain. Shaking is therefore not destruction for its own sake; it is a sorting. There is also a shaking of blessing and confirmation: after the church prayed, “the place was shaken where they were assembled together; and they were all filled with the Holy Ghost” (Act 4:31) — God answering a prayer for boldness by moving the building. And there is the shaking of generous measure: “good measure, pressed down, and shaken together, and running over” (Luk 6:38), the grain settled by shaking so that more can be added. Judgment, confirmation, and generosity all reach for the same verb.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines shake as to cause to move with quick vibrations, to agitate, to make to totter or tremble, and to throw down by a violent motion.

expand to see more

SHAKE, v.t. To cause to move with quick vibrations; to move rapidly one way and the other; to agitate.

2. To make to totter or tremble.

3. To throw down by a violent motion; as, to shake down fruit.

4. To move from firmness; to weaken the stability of; to endanger; to threaten to overthrow.

5. To drive from a resolution, or to cause to waver.

Key Scripture

Hag 2:6 — "For thus saith the LORD of hosts; Yet once, it is a little while, and I will shake the heavens, and the earth, and the sea, and the dry land;"

Heb 12:26 — "Whose voice then shook the earth: but now he hath promised, saying, Yet once more I shake not the earth only, but also heaven."

Act 4:31 — "And when they had prayed, the place was shaken where they were assembled together; and they were all filled with the Holy Ghost, and they spake the word of God with boldness."

Luk 6:38 — "Give, and it shall be given unto you; good measure, pressed down, and shaken together, and running over, shall men give into your bosom. For with the same measure that ye mete withal it shall be measured to you again."

Modern Corruption

Upheaval is read as evidence that God has lost control, when Hebrews presents the shaking as His own deliberate sorting of what will stand from what was never founded.

expand to see more

When institutions fall, reputations collapse, and long-settled certainties give way, the reflex of unbelief is to conclude that no one is steering. Hebrews 12 makes the shaking itself an act of the same voice that spoke at Sinai, and gives its purpose: the removing of what is made, that the things which cannot be shaken may remain. A believer watching things fall is watching a divine sifting, not a divine absence — and the practical question is never why God allowed the shaking but what in one's own life was resting on shakable ground.

The chapter's conclusion is not stoic endurance but worship: wherefore we receiving a kingdom which cannot be moved, let us have grace, whereby we may serve God acceptably with reverence and godly fear. The unshakable thing already given is a kingdom. So Acts 4 fits: the church prays under threat, the room shakes, and what comes out of it is boldness in speech. God shakes the walls and steadies the men.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew ra'ash (H7493), to quake, shake, tremble; Greek seiō (G4579) and saleuō (G4531), to shake or agitate — the sorting of what stands.

expand to see more

Hebrew ra'ash (H7493) — to quake or shake; “I will shake the heavens, and the earth” (Hag 2:6).

Greek seiō (G4579) — to shake, agitate; the root behind seismos, an earthquake.

Greek saleuō (G4531) — to shake or make to totter; used in Heb 12:27 of the things that are shaken and removed.

Usage

"“Yet once more I shake not the earth only, but also heaven” — the last sorting announced in advance."

"“The place was shaken where they were assembled” — God answering a prayer for boldness."

"“Pressed down, and shaken together, and running over” — measure settled so more can be given."
